title: EADDRINUSE
jokes: Port {port} is already taken. By you. Twenty minutes ago.
Something's already squatting on port {port} and it's probably your last unkilled process.
EADDRINUSE: port {port} called dibs first.
You started this server so many times port {port} filed a restraining order.
Port {port} is occupied. Have you tried turning it off? The old one, I mean.
There's a zombie process on port {port} and only you can kill it.

fix.summary: Find and kill the process holding the port, or use a different port.

sarcastic-senior-dev: Port {port} is taken. Probably by the zombie process from your last crash. kill it and move on.
EADDRINUSE on {port}. This is the fourth time this week, isn't it.

title: Cannot find module
jokes: '{module_name}' isn't installed. node_modules remains a mystery box.
You required '{module_name}' on pure faith.
Cannot find module '{module_name}': have you tried it existing?
'{module_name}' is not in node_modules, which continues to be a 40,000-file black hole with nothing you need.
Node looked for '{module_name}' and came back empty-handed.
This module was never installed. This is the whole problem.

fix.summary: Install the missing package.

sarcastic-senior-dev: '{module_name}' isn't installed. Run the install command. I promise it's still npm install.
Missing module '{module_name}'. Did you even run npm install after pulling?

title: TypeError: x is not a function
jokes: '{expr}' is not a function. It's not anything, really.
You called '{expr}()' like it was going to do something.
'{expr}' is not a function, it's a cry for help.
TypeError: '{expr}' never agreed to be callable.
This is what happens when you assume the import worked.

fix.summary: Check the import/require is correct and the value is actually a function.

sarcastic-senior-dev: '{expr}' is not a function. Maybe check what it actually is before calling it next time.
Calling '{expr}' like it's a function was optimistic. It wasn't.

title: Cannot read properties of undefined
jokes: You reached into undefined looking for '.{prop}'. It wasn't there. Nothing was there.
'.{prop}' of undefined: the most-filed bug report in JavaScript history.
undefined doesn't have properties. This is not new information.
You assumed that value existed. JavaScript disagreed, loudly.
This is basically JavaScript's national anthem at this point.

fix.summary: Add a null/undefined check or optional chaining before accessing the property.

title: UnhandledPromiseRejection
jokes: You threw a promise into the void with no .catch() to save it.
This promise rejected and nobody was there to hear it.
UnhandledPromiseRejection: async code, unhandled consequences.
You forgot the .catch(). Every time. Forever.
This is what happens when await doesn't get a try/catch.

fix.summary: Add a .catch() handler or wrap the await in try/catch.

sarcastic-senior-dev: No .catch(), no try/catch, no plan. This is why we do code review.
An unhandled rejection. I've flagged this exact pattern in every PR you've ever sent me.

title: SyntaxError: Unexpected token
jokes: Node choked on '{token}'. Fair reaction, honestly.
SyntaxError: '{token}' was not invited to this parse.
'{token}' broke the parser. Impressive, in a bad way.
That token is in the wrong place, wrong file, or wrong universe.
Node saw '{token}' and gave up immediately.

fix.summary: Check for a stray character, missing bracket, or unsupported syntax for your Node version.

title: ENOENT
jokes: '{path}' does not exist, and Node would like you to know that.
ENOENT: '{path}' is a path to nowhere.
That file at '{path}' is fictional.
Node went looking for '{path}' and found only disappointment.
'{path}' — this file has never existed, and it shows.

fix.summary: Verify the file path is correct relative to the process's working directory.

title: npm ERR! peer dep conflict
jokes: Two packages want mutually exclusive versions of the same dependency. Classic.
npm found a peer dependency conflict and refused to guess for you.
ERESOLVE: your dependency tree has trust issues.
This is what happens when the ecosystem has forty versions of everything.
npm is asking you to pick a side in a fight it started.

fix.summary: Resolve the conflicting versions, or use --legacy-peer-deps if you understand the risk.

title: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded

matcher.pattern: RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded

jokes: Your function called itself until the stack gave up.
Maximum call stack size exceeded: infinite recursion strikes again.
This function will not stop calling itself. It needs a base case, and an intervention.
The call stack has a limit. You found it.
Somewhere, a recursive function forgot how to stop.

fix.summary: Add or fix the base case that should terminate the recursion.

sarcastic-senior-dev: Infinite recursion, no base case. A tale as old as time, or at least as old as this codebase.
Stack overflow from recursion. Check your base case. It's always the base case.

title: CORS error

matcher.pattern: has been blocked by CORS policy

jokes: CORS just said no, and it will keep saying no until you configure it properly.
The browser is protecting you from yourself, and it's very annoying about it.
CORS: the security feature everyone learns to hate the hard way.
Your server didn't send the right headers, so the browser blocked the party.
This is CORS working exactly as designed, which is the worst part.

fix.summary: Add the correct Access-Control-Allow-Origin header on the server.

title: Jest: no tests found

matcher.pattern: No tests found, exiting with code 1

jokes: Jest looked for tests and found the same nothing your coverage report already knew about.
No tests found. Bold strategy.
Your test suite is theoretical at this point.
Jest came up empty. So did your confidence in this code.
There is a testPathPattern mismatch, or there are just no tests. Pick your truth.

fix.summary: Check your testMatch/testPathPattern config or that test files exist.

title: JavaScript heap out of memory

matcher.pattern: FATAL ERROR: .*JavaScript heap out of memory

jokes: Node ran out of memory trying to hold whatever you built.
The heap is out of memory. So is your patience, probably.
You built something so large V8 had to tap out.
This process needs more RAM than it was given, and it wants you to know.
Heap out of memory: the sound of a memory leak reaching its final form.

fix.summary: Increase Node's heap size or find the memory leak.

title: ECONNREFUSED
jokes: Nothing is listening on {host}:{port}. Did you forget to start it?
Connection refused to {host}:{port} — that service is not home.
You're trying to talk to {host}:{port} and it's not picking up.
ECONNREFUSED: {host}:{port} wants nothing to do with you right now.
That server on {host}:{port} either crashed or was never started.

fix.summary: Make sure the target service is actually running on that host/port.

title: TypeScript type error
jokes: TypeScript says: '{message}'. It's not wrong.
The type checker caught you: '{message}'.
TypeScript is doing its one job: '{message}'.
This is exactly why you added TypeScript. '{message}'.
The compiler disagrees with your life choices: '{message}'.

fix.summary: Fix the type mismatch reported by the compiler.

title: TypeError: Cannot destructure property of undefined

matcher.pattern: TypeError: Cannot destructure property '(\w+)' of '.*' as it is undefined

jokes: You destructured '.{prop}' from undefined. Undefined does not have properties.
This is Cannot-read-property's cooler cousin, same underlying problem.
You assumed that object existed before pulling '{prop}' out of it.
Destructuring undefined is still just accessing undefined, with extra syntax.
'{prop}' was never going to come out of nothing.
The value you're destructuring never arrived, and neither did '{prop}'.

fix.summary: Add a default value or null check before destructuring.

title: ERR_REQUIRE_ESM
jokes: You require()'d a package that only speaks ESM now.
This module went all-in on import/export and left require() behind.
ERR_REQUIRE_ESM: the CommonJS/ESM divide claims another victim.
That package dropped CommonJS support and nobody warned your require() calls.
You're mixing module systems and Node is refusing to referee.
This is the tax for depending on a package that modernized before you did.

fix.summary: Use a dynamic import() instead of require(), or switch the project to ESM.

title: EPERM: operation not permitted
jokes: Node tried to {operation} '{path}' and the OS said absolutely not.
EPERM: '{path}' is locked, watched, or owned by something else entirely.
Something else has '{path}' open, and it isn't sharing.
You tried to {operation} '{path}' without the permissions to back it up.
This is the classic 'another process is using this file' problem, spelled EPERM.
'{path}' is not yours to {operation} right now.

fix.summary: Close any process holding the file open, or fix its permissions.

title: self-signed certificate error
jokes: Node doesn't trust that certificate, and honestly it has a point.
This TLS chain ends in a cert nobody vouched for.
Self-signed certificate: convenient for dev, terrifying for trust chains.
Node's TLS verification just caught something you were hoping it wouldn't notice.
That certificate signed itself. Node finds that suspicious, correctly.
This is what happens in local dev with a cert nobody in the real world trusts.

fix.summary: Use a properly signed cert, or set NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED only for local dev.

title: webpack: Module not found

matcher.pattern: Module not found: Error: Can't resolve '([^']+)'

jokes: webpack went looking for '{module_name}' and came back empty.
'{module_name}' isn't installed, or the path to it is wrong. Pick one.
This is the bundler's version of ModuleNotFoundError, and it means the same thing.
webpack can't resolve '{module_name}' because it genuinely isn't there.
'{module_name}' was imported into existence but never actually installed.
The bundler cannot bundle what does not exist.

fix.summary: Install the missing package or fix the import path.

title: Invalid hook call

matcher.pattern: Invalid hook call\. Hooks can only be called

jokes: You called a hook somewhere React did not expect a hook to be called.
Hooks have rules. You broke one of the two rules there are.
This is either a conditional hook, a loop hook, or two copies of React fighting.
React's rules of hooks exist specifically to prevent this error.
Somewhere, a hook was called outside a function component and React noticed immediately.
You either called this hook conditionally, or you have duplicate React versions installed.

fix.summary: Check for conditional hook calls, or duplicate React versions in node_modules.

title: Unexpected token in JSON

matcher.pattern: Unexpected token .* in JSON at position \d+

jokes: Something you're parsing as JSON is not JSON. A trailing comma, probably.
JSON.parse() met your string and immediately gave up.
This is what a stray comma or an HTML error page disguised as JSON looks like.
Whatever came back was not valid JSON, no matter how confident you were.
The JSON parser found the exact character it hates most.
This usually means the response body isn't what you thought it was.

fix.summary: Log the raw string before parsing to see what was actually returned.

title: TypeError: fetch failed
jokes: fetch() tried to reach something and came back with nothing but disappointment.
This is DNS, network, or a dead server, wearing a very unhelpful error message.
fetch failed: somewhere between here and the destination, something gave up.
The network request didn't just fail, it failed to even tell you why clearly.
You're offline, the host is down, or the URL is wrong. Take your pick.
This is the generic wrapper error hiding the actual network problem underneath.

fix.summary: Check network connectivity, the target URL, and DNS resolution.

title: listen EACCES: permission denied
jokes: Binding to {host}:{port} needs privileges you don't currently have.
Ports below 1024 belong to root. You are not root.
This is the OS telling you to pick a higher port number, politely, via crashing.
{host}:{port} is a privileged port and your process is not privileged.
You'll need sudo or a different port. Pick the less scary option.
listen EACCES: the classic 'trying to bind to port 80 as a regular user' story.

fix.summary: Use a port above 1024, or grant the process permission to bind to privileged ports.

title: SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module

matcher.pattern: SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module

jokes: You used import syntax in a file Node still thinks is CommonJS.
This file needs to be told it's an ES module. It currently believes otherwise.
import/export doesn't work here until package.json says "type": "module".
Node parsed this as CommonJS and choked on the first import statement it found.
You wrote modern syntax into a file running under old module rules.
This is a module-type mismatch, not a real syntax error.

fix.summary: Add "type": "module" to package.json, or use .mjs, or switch to require().

title: TypeError: x is not iterable
jokes: You tried to spread or for-of a '{expr}' that has no idea what iteration is.
'{expr}' is not iterable, because it was never an array, Map, or Set to begin with.
This is what happens when a function you expected to return an array returns something else.
You can't for-of over '{expr}'. It doesn't have that ability.
'{expr}' lacks a Symbol.iterator, and so does your assumption about its type.
Spread syntax needs something iterable. '{expr}' was not the something you thought it was.

fix.summary: Check the actual type/shape of the value before iterating over it.

title: Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client

matcher.pattern: Error: Can't set headers after they are sent to the client

jokes: You called res.send() twice on the same request. The client already left.
This response already went out the door. Setting headers now is too late.
Somewhere in this handler, a response is being sent more than once.
Express is telling you politely that you double-responded to a single request.
The client already got its response. Whatever you're trying to send now, it's not listening.
This is the classic missing-return-statement-after-res.send() bug.

fix.summary: Make sure every code path returns after sending a response, so it only sends once.

title: MaxListenersExceededWarning
jokes: This EventEmitter has more listeners attached to it than seems healthy.
Node thinks you have a memory leak. Node is probably right.
Something is calling .on() in a loop without ever calling .off().
MaxListenersExceededWarning: your event emitter is quietly accumulating listeners forever.
This is the warning before the memory leak becomes a real problem.
Somewhere, a listener is being added on every request and never removed.

fix.summary: Find where listeners are added repeatedly and remove them, or raise the limit deliberately.

title: RangeError: Invalid array length
jokes: You asked for an array with a length that doesn't make sense. Negative, probably.
Arrays cannot have negative or absurdly large lengths, no matter how you calculated it.
Something upstream produced a bad number, and now new Array() is paying for it.
RangeError: Invalid array length. Check the math that produced that length.
This is what happens when a length calculation goes negative or infinite.
That array length came from somewhere broken. Follow it back.

fix.summary: Check the calculation that produced the array length before constructing it.

title: ReferenceError: Buffer is not defined
jokes: Buffer is a Node global. You're not in Node anymore, or your bundler stripped it.
This code assumed a Node environment. It's running somewhere else now.
Buffer doesn't exist in the browser, and modern bundlers stopped polyfilling it for you.
You ported Node code to the browser and Buffer didn't come along for the ride.
This is the price of bundlers dropping automatic Node polyfills.
Buffer used to be quietly polyfilled. Those days are over.

fix.summary: Add a Buffer polyfill for the browser, or avoid Buffer usage in client code.

title: ReferenceError: process is not defined
jokes: process is a Node global. This code is not running in Node.
You're using process.env in a place that has no process at all.
This is what happens when server code sneaks into a browser bundle unmodified.
process doesn't exist in the browser, and your bundler didn't shim it this time.
Someone wrote isomorphic code that was not, in fact, isomorphic.
process.env is a Node concept. The browser has never heard of it.

fix.summary: Use build-time env injection (e.g. define plugin) instead of relying on process at runtime in the browser.
